sentences.text: Eolambia is classified as a large hadrosauroid dinosaur.
This animal could measure up to 6 meters in length and weigh approximately 1 metric ton.
Another adult specimen was estimated in 2008 to be 5.2 meters long with a hip height of 2 meters.
It possessed a crestless skull with a shape similar to those of Equijubus and Probactrosaurus.
In 1979, Peter Galton and James A. Jensen described a fragmentary femur of a hadrosaurian from the Cedar Mountain Formation in Arches National Park, Utah.
Later, Carole Jones and Ramal Jones discovered fragmentary bones of Eolambia in 1993 at a site in the northwestern San Rafael Swell.
The type specimen of Eolambia was discovered by Carole and Ramal Jones in 1993.
Specimen CEUM 9758 represents partial remains of an adult hadrosauroid including skull parts, vertebrae, ischium, and leg.
Eolambia lived in humid floodplain forests near lakes and ate gymnosperms, ferns, and flowering plants.
Juvenile Eolambia were preyed upon by large crocodylomorphs living in lake waters.
Mature Eolambia individuals, at least eight to nine years old, were preyed upon by large theropods like Siats.
The genus name Eolambia combines the Greek word for dawn with a suffix derived from Lambeosaurus.
In its initial description, Eolambia was classified as a member of the Hadrosauridae family.
Eolambia may be more closely related to Protohadros, forming an isolated radiation of hadrosauroids based on skull and shoulder bone traits.
Similarities between Eolambia and lambeosaurine hadrosaurids are considered either convergent evolution or misinterpretations.
Eolambia lived during the Cenomanian stage.
A 1997 study dated a volcanic ash layer in the formation containing Eolambia to 97 ± 0.1 million years ago.
Agreement between dating estimates indicates that Eolambia lived during the Cenomanian stage.
Eolambia fossils are found exclusively in the Mussentuchit Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation.
Researchers caution that a specimen with an unusually deep dentary might represent a distinct hadrosauroid rather than Eolambia.
Kirkland debated whether Eolambia was a basal member of the Lambeosaurinae or their sister group.
Jason Head concluded that Eolambia belongs to the Hadrosauroidea but is outside the Hadrosauridae family.
